national_day.intro: Singapore's National Day on 9 August celebrates the nation's independence in 1965.
national_day.history: On 9 August 1965 Singapore separated from Malaysia and became an independent, sovereign republic. From a small port city it grew rapidly into one of the world's wealthiest nations, a transformation celebrated each year.
national_day.traditions: The highlight is the National Day Parade, with military and civilian processions, an air force flypast and a spectacular fireworks display over Marina Bay. Singaporeans recite the National Pledge and sing along to a specially commissioned theme song.
funFacts: It marks Singapore's 1965 separation from Malaysia.
The National Day Parade features a dramatic flypast and fireworks.
Reciting the National Pledge together is part of the National Day celebrations.

chinese_new_year.intro: Chinese New Year is one of Singapore's biggest festivals, a two-day public holiday welcoming the lunar new year.
chinese_new_year.history: Brought by Chinese immigrants who form the majority of Singapore's population, Chinese New Year marks the start of the lunar calendar. Over generations it has become a defining national celebration in multicultural Singapore.
chinese_new_year.traditions: Families gather for reunion dinners and toss "yusheng", a prosperity salad, for good luck. Chinatown is decorated with lights, children receive red packets (hongbao), and lion dances are performed for prosperity.
funFacts: Tossing "yusheng" salad higher is said to bring greater fortune.
Red packets called "hongbao" contain money for luck.
Chinatown's annual light-up draws huge crowds.

deepavali.intro: Deepavali, the Festival of Lights, is an important Hindu celebration and a public holiday in Singapore. Lamps and family gatherings express the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil.
deepavali.history: Deepavali has roots in several Hindu traditions, whose stories and practices vary by community. In Singapore, Tamil and other Indian communities have made it an important part of the country’s cultural life. Its calendar date changes from year to year.
deepavali.traditions: Families clean their homes, decorate doorways with oil lamps and kolam patterns, and visit temples and relatives. New clothes, sweets and shared meals are part of the celebration. Little India is known for its festive street decorations and markets.
funFacts: The name Deepavali refers to a row of lights.
Kolam patterns may be made with coloured rice powder.
Singapore’s celebrations reflect the traditions of its local Hindu communities.

vesak_day.intro: Vesak Day is a Buddhist celebration and a public holiday in Singapore. It commemorates the Buddha’s birth, enlightenment and passing into final nirvana, particularly in Theravada tradition.
vesak_day.history: Vesak takes its name from a month of the traditional Indian calendar. Buddhist communities observe its events in different ways and sometimes on different dates. In Singapore, the occasion brings together temple worship, reflection and acts of generosity.
vesak_day.traditions: Devotees visit temples, offer flowers and lights, and listen to teachings. Some temples hold ceremonies bathing a small image of the infant Buddha. Giving to charity, volunteering and sharing vegetarian meals express compassion in everyday life.
funFacts: Flowers in temple offerings can symbolise the impermanence of life.
Practices differ among Singapore’s Buddhist communities.
The Gregorian date changes with the calendar used to determine the observance.
